item.title: C++ Associative Containers: Enabling Heterogeneous Lookups via Transparent Comparators
item.description:
“C++ Associative Containers: Enabling Heterogeneous Lookups via Transparent Comparators”

A significant enhancement arrived in C++14 concerning associative containers like std::set and std::map. This change introduced member function template overloads for lookup operations (find, lower_bound, etc.), allowing searches using types other than the container’s precise key type. However, this feature required a specific mechanism to activate safely, avoiding potential performance pitfalls or breakage in existing codebases.

How Does Heterogeneous Lookup Functionality Work and Does It Alter Default Container Behavior?

Fundamentally, the addition of member function templates allows you to query a container using a type comparable to the key type, rather than strictly requiring the key_type.

item.title: C++ emplace_back vs push_back Performance and Variadic Templates
item.description:
“C++ emplace_back vs push_back Performance and Variadic Templates”

Why is the C++0x emplace_back(Args&&...) Signature Significant?

The function signature void emplace_back(Args&&...) introduced in C++0x (C++11) is particularly impactful. Instead of accepting a fully formed value_type, it accepts a parameter pack of arguments. This design allows the container to perfectly forward these arguments straight to the constructor of the element type being placed inside the container. This direct construction avoids creating any intermediate temporary objects, leading to performance gains, especially for complex types.

item.title: C++ Stream Output: Effective Ways to Join Container Elements with Separators
item.description:
“C++ Stream Output: Effective Ways to Join Container Elements with Separators”

A multitude of strategies exist, ranging from low-level iterator adjustments to utilizing newer library features.

Custom Iterator Implementation: The infix_ostream_iterator

A highly effective C++ solution involves crafting a custom output iterator, inspired by the standard std::ostream_iterator, but designed to insert the delimiter before every element except the very first one. This pattern, often attributed to experts like Jerry Coffin, places the separator logic within the assignment operator of the iterator.

item.title: C++: Storing References in STL Containers Like std::vector
item.description:
“C++: Storing References in STL Containers Like std::vector”

The inability to place non-assignable types, specifically references, directly into standard containers stems from core C++ language rules regarding references and container mechanics.

The Core Restriction on References in Containers

A fundamental aspect of C++ references is that they must be initialized when declared, and they cannot be reseated to refer to a different object afterward.

Consider this fundamental behavior:

int b_value = 10;
int c_value = 20;

int & a_ref = b_value; // a_ref is an alias for b_value
a_ref = c_value;      // This assigns the VALUE of c_value (20) to b_value.
                      // a_ref still refers to b_value.
